government-impersonation: Someone poses as police, a court, immigration or another government office and threatens arrest, deportation or fines unless you pay or hand over personal details.
investment: A stranger or online friend promotes an investment, often crypto or stocks, shows fake profits and gets you to send more and more money.
business-email-compromise: A message that looks like it is from your boss, a colleague or a supplier asks you to move money, change payment details or share staff records.
recovery: After you lose money to a scam, someone poses as a lawyer, agency or recovery firm and charges a fee to get it back.
tech-support: A pop-up, call or email claims your computer or account has a problem, then a fake support agent takes remote access and moves your money.
charity-donation: A fake charity or campaign asks for donations after a disaster, during a crisis or at election time.
extortion: Someone threatens to expose, hurt or embarrass you or the people close to you, using personal details they found, unless you pay.
phishing: A message copies a real organisation and sends you to a fake login page to steal your password or account.
job-offer: A recruiter or employer offers easy remote work, then asks for fees, your bank details or to move money for them.
online-shopping: A fake shop, advert or seller takes payment for goods that never arrive.
sextortion: Someone threatens to share real or faked intimate images of you with your family and friends unless you pay.
identity-theft: Someone uses your personal details, such as birthday, address and employer, to open accounts, file documents or pass checks in your name.
bank-impersonation: A caller or text poses as your bank's fraud team, says your account is at risk and gets you to move money or read out a code.
romance: Someone builds a relationship with you on a dating app or social media, then asks for money or gets you to pay for something.
account-takeover: Someone answers your security questions, tricks support staff or sends you a link to reset your password and take over your email or other accounts.
swatting: Someone uses your home address and phone number to send police to your door with a false emergency report.
known-contact-impersonation: A text or voice message pretends to be someone you know or work with, sometimes with a cloned voice, to get you onto another app or to click a link.
payroll-diversion: A fake staff portal or email steals your work login and reroutes your pay.
family-emergency: Someone calls or texts your family pretending to be you or a relative in trouble, in jail or in an accident, and asks for urgent money.
money-mule: You are recruited, through a job or a relationship, to receive and pass on money for criminals.
fake-website: A copy of a real website takes payments or collects personal details.
virtual-kidnapping: Someone sends your family altered photos of you as proof they are holding you and demands a ransom.
qr-phishing: An unexpected parcel or notice carries a QR code that leads to a page that steals your details.
health-insurer-impersonation: A message poses as a health insurer or investigator and asks for medical records, account details or a repayment.
health-insurance: A caller sells a cheap health plan that turns out not to be insurance.
ai-impersonation: Someone clones your voice or face from public videos and photos and uses it to ask your family or contacts for money.
crypto-exchange-impersonation: A caller poses as your crypto exchange, says your account is compromised and gets your login or a transfer.
toll-smishing: A text says you owe a small road toll or delivery fee and links to a page that takes your card details.
timeshare: Someone offers to sell or rent out a timeshare you own and charges upfront fees.
student-loan: A call, text or email about student loan forgiveness or financial aid asks for a fee, your login or your personal details.
sim-swap: Someone uses your personal details to move your phone number to their SIM, then receives your login codes.
crypto-atm-payment: A caller keeps you on the phone and directs you to pay through a crypto cash machine or QR code.
boss-gift-cards: A message that appears to come from your boss, professor or someone in authority asks you to buy gift cards and send the codes.
rental: A fake landlord or listing for a flat or room near you asks for a deposit, an application fee or your details before you have seen the place.
financial-aid: A call or message about unpaid tuition, a refund or financial aid says you must pay or confirm your details now or lose your place.
prize: A call, letter or message says you won a prize, sweepstakes or unclaimed money and asks for a fee or your bank details to release it.
debt-relief: A caller promises to wipe or cut your debt for an upfront fee.
pet-sale: A fake advert for a puppy, kitten or exotic pet takes payment, then keeps asking for shipping and vet fees.
lost-pet: After you post about a lost or sick pet, someone claims to have it or to be treating it and asks for payment.
travel: A fake travel site, deal or booking takes payment for a trip, visa or document service that is not real.
grant: A message offers free government money or help with bills and asks for a fee or your personal details first.
utility: A caller or visitor poses as your power, gas or water company and threatens to cut you off unless you pay at once.
loan: A call or text follows up on a loan you never applied for to get your personal and bank details.
immigration: Someone on social media poses as an immigration lawyer or official and charges for help with visas or status.
funeral-impersonation: After a death in the family is made public, someone poses as the funeral home or an official and tells relatives to pay now.
